title: Bullet train long noses aren't actually for wind drag? | So That's Why
description:
Stand on a platform as a high-speed train glides in, and the first thing that catches your eye is its long, pointed nose. Most people assume it's stretched out to cut wind drag, yet what rail engineers really dread is a loud "boom" bursting from a tunnel exit kilometers away. Even more counterintuitively, Taiwan's 700T has a higher design top speed, yet its nose shrinks to just 8 meters. Why?

For anyone whose ears have popped entering a railway tunnel, who wonders why Shinkansen noses look like duckbills or kingfishers, or who wants to know what changed on Taiwan's new N700ST.

This episode unpacks the split second a train plunges into a tunnel: why the Sanyo Shinkansen set off tunnel micro-pressure waves in 1975, how paraboloids, projectiles fired into narrow pipes, and a supercomputer arrived at a kingfisher-like 15-meter nose, and why engineers later shrank the 700 Series back to 9.2 meters—and Taiwan's 700T down to 8 meters thanks to tunnels nearly 50% wider—to win back passenger seats. (Note: Official specs do not publish standalone nose lengths in meters for the N700 series or N700ST, so this video explains them via the 27,350 mm lead-car length and Dual Supreme Wing profile; 500 Series retirement dates follow JR West's current schedule.)

Illustrations in this episode were generated with AI.

Information as of 2026-11-18

p001.text: Train glides in; two models in hand—Chief, why that long nose?

p002.text: Taiwan's 700T is faster, yet shorter than Japan's?

p003.text: Inside tunnels: in 1975, a far exit boomed right on entry?

p005.text: Crazy part: it's not mainly wind drag!

p007.text: Hand out a car window, wind pushes back—so we assume wind drag;

p008.text: Yeah, like a knife slicing the air?

p009.text: A sleek nose cuts some drag, but Japan's RTRI measured a whole Shinkansen:

p010.text: with over a dozen cars, most drag clings to sides and gaps!

p011.text: Side friction and gap eddies stack up; the nose share is modest;

p012.text: On open plains, you need no 10-meter-plus nose.

p013.text: What forced long noses is that tunnel turning windows black!

p014.text: In a tunnel, can't air dodge sideways?

p015.text: Outdoors, air can flee in every direction;

p016.text: Yet a tunnel is a sealed stone pipe: air is trapped!

p017.text: Speeding in is like slamming a bike-pump piston:

p018.text: trapped air squeezes into a compression wave!

p019.text: That wave races down the sealed tunnel way faster than the train,

p020.text: just in, the wave hits the exit kilometers away!

p021.text: Shooting out, it fires a pressure pulse—BOOM!

p022.text: RTRI says micro-pressure wave: Japan's "don," or "tunnel boom."

p023.text: A boom? Does it go supersonic inside?

p024.text: Not supersonic! Per NASA, sound at sea level travels about 1,225 km/h;

p025.text: even at 300 km/h, it's a quarter Mach; the wave's four times faster.

p026.text: The air wave hits sound speed, not the train itself!

p027.text: Scholar Saito Sanetoshi notes: strong above 20 Hz, it booms like cannon;

p028.text: Below that, ears may miss it, yet home windows rattle hard!

p029.text: But the first Shinkansen ran in 1964—

p030.text: remember that 1975 boom? Why did a new line blast 11 years later?

p031.text: It's the track! Ozawa Satoru and Saito note old tunnels used gravel beds,

p032.text: Pebble gaps act like a sponge, dulling the wave.

p033.text: But Sanyo's Okayama-Hakata line laid hard, flat concrete slabs,

p034.text: so waves pile steeper down long tunnels and blast at the exit!

p035.text: Worse, expert Harada Iwao showed: wind drag scales as speed squared,

p036.text: but micro-waves pass speed cubed; noise hits power six!

p037.text: Just 10% more speed boosts that boom over 30%!

p038.text: We can't move mountains! How do we hush it?

p038b.text: Can't move mountains, so engineers reshaped the nose!

p039.text: Does a long nose suck air in like a sponge?

p040.text: Solid metal won't suck air! RTRI tests and math found the key:

p041.text: Boom size depends on entry steepness: pressure gradient!

p042.text: Think: a blunt nose slams in, spiking pressure sky-high;

p043.text: lengthen the tip so its cross-section widens bit by bit,

p044.text: and that cliff flattens, shrinking the exit boom!

p045.text: So is a sharp cone the best?

p046.text: RTRI tested a round egg-nose, a sharp cone, and a spun paraboloid!

p047.text: Harada Iwao showed cone area surges aft, still shoving air;

p048.text: only a paraboloid adds area evenly at every moment,

p049.text: giving the lowest peak gradient of all three!

p050.text: They also lowered roofs into a slimmer, rounder body,

p051.text: blocking less tunnel, shoving less air, dropping waves more!

p052.text: Does the nose carry it all, tunnels as-is?

p053.text: Tunnels help too! Most slab-track portals in Japan wear hoods.

p054.text: Long slotted hoods vent air in stages before the main tunnel!

p055.text: With noses and hoods on, remember protests 400 meters out? Why the noise?

p056.text: Speed jumped again! Remember 300 km/h? JR West wanted passenger runs on Sanyo;

p057.text: 500 Series test lead Nakatsu Eiji wrote: 51% of Sanyo is tunnels,

p058.text: and Japan's 65 m² tunnels fit a 3.4-meter car tight like needle in pipe!

p059.text: Nakatsu recalled low waves made residents 400 meters out complain,

p060.text: forcing the team to drop tests above 350 km/h!

p061.text: Stuck, a young engineer said: entering, the train feels squeezed smaller!

p062.text: Birdwatcher Nakatsu asked: who dives daily from thin air into dense water?

p064.text: Yes! Kingfishers dive for fish; drag spikes, yet the splash is tiny.

p065.text: So they traced its beak with a ruler?

p066.text: Many think so, yet it's reversed—a spark first, then tests computed it!

p067.text: They fired bullets into pipes, then simulated tunnels on a supercomputer,

p068.text: and the ideal area curve closely matched a kingfisher's beak to head!

p069.text: A 2019 study tested 71 kingfisher species, proving this shape cuts drag!

p070.text: They also copied owl-feather serrations on pantographs to hush wind noise.

p071.text: March 1997: sporting a 15-meter nose, round 500 Series joined Sanyo—

p072.text: remember that Sanyo goal? It became Japan's first Shinkansen to hit it!

p073.text: Shin-Osaka-Hakata fell 15 min; Nakatsu saw 10%-plus saved on 300 Series;

p074.text: Per JR West's current plan, regular runs end Jan 13, 2027, retiring that July.

p075.text: So cool! Did newer Shinkansen get even longer?

p076.text: Just the opposite! Next up, 700 Series shrank back to 9.2 meters!

p077.text: Wait—why stretch it, then chop it?

p078.text: Car length is fixed: a longer nose eats up cab room and seats!

p079.text: Per Ishizuka Osamu and Toyo Keizai, shared runs needed same seats and doors,

p080.text: so blended paraboloids made a wide flat nose, taming waves at 285 km/h!

p081.text: No wonder that wide duckbill look—it's winning seats!

p082.text: Right! On the later N700S, the lead car stays at 27,350 mm—not 1 mm added—

p083.text: raising twin side ridges into the Dual Supreme Wing shape,

p084.text: cutting tunnel waves while smoothing tail vortices to reduce sway!

p085.text: Here's the twist: Tohoku hit 320 km/h—remember 15 meters? E5 Series went back!

p086.text: Chasing 360 km/h, test train ALFA-X tests 16- and 22-meter noses on both ends!

p087.text: In 2019, RTRI built a 3-stage curve, trimming a 12-meter test nose by a meter!

p088.text: To rail engineers, every nose meter is a tug-of-war with seats!

p090.text: Faster top speed than Japan's—why shrink to 8 meters?

p091.text: Tunnel width! Ishizuka Osamu wrote: remember 700 Series? 700T came from it,

p092.text: but Taiwan built tunnels over 90 m²—nearly 50% bigger than Japan's!

p093.text: Wider bores give air plenty of room to slip past, so waves start weaker!

p094.text: Japan's mechanical society notes Taiwan's 30-to-40-meter, 45° hoods,

p095.text: with side vents and roof shafts gently bleeding pressure—

p096.text: remember asking why it's shorter? Tunnels share the load, sparing the nose!

p097.text: How will Taiwan's new train nose look?

p098.text: On Aug 15, 2026, Taiwan's first next-gen set reached Kaohsiung—

p099.text: remember twin-wing noses and wide bores? N700ST pairs them for late-2027 service!

p100.text: Next time on the platform, spot those twin wing-like side ridges,

p101.text: and remember Taiwan's slanted hoods? Spot them from a window seat!

p102.text: Standing here it clicks—remember me comparing my two models?

p103.text: There's no single answer—every meter balances route and cabin space!

p105.text: Do your ears pop in tunnels? Favorite nose? Tell us in comments!
